ref.start.title: Getting started
ref.start.intro: In Arcadeer, everything that appears in your game is an object. Each object corresponds to one CoffeeScript class.
ref.start.d1: Creating a project gives you gameMain.coffee. Your game starts here. Set the screen size, then place what you need with addObject.
ref.start.d2: Use "Add new" to create a class file. behavior runs every frame, so put the movement there.
ref.start.d3: Built-in shapes such as box and sphere can be placed directly, with no class file.
ref.basics.title: Core ideas
ref.basics.d.axis: Right-handed, with Y as the up axis. Z is depth, and positive Z points toward the viewer.
ref.basics.d.object: One class file in the code directory is one kind of object. All of them extend arcadeermain, and addObject creates instances. Instances go into the object list and are processed in that order every frame.
ref.basics.d.frame: Each frame runs the steps below. Spare time is spent waiting; if the work runs long, the swap waits until it finishes. Heavy frames never skip ahead — the whole game simply slows down.
ref.frame.1: Walk the object list and call behavior on each one
ref.frame.3: Wait until the frame time has passed
ref.frame.4: Swap the front and back buffers
ref.basics.d.kind: Set with @KIND. If you omit it, the kind is decided from @MODEL.
ref.kind.none: Not drawn; for logic only (such as gameMain)
ref.basics.d.prim: Usable without a 3D model. Each fits in a 1 × 1 × 1 box centred on the origin, so use SCALEX and friends to set the size.
ref.col.name: Name
ref.api.title: API reference
ref.api.d.params: Every object has these. Read and write them inside behavior.
ref.p.vel: Velocity, added to the position every frame
ref.p.gravity: Gravity. A positive value pulls downward
ref.p.rot: Rotation around each axis, in degrees. Applied Z, then X, then Y
ref.p.model: Model name or asset file name
ref.p.color: Draw colour. Empty keeps the original colours
ref.p.shadow: Whether this object casts a shadow
ref.p.proc: Status number, free for you to use
ref.m.addObject: Create an object, add it to the list, and return the reference
ref.m.waitjob: Wait for the given time, then move to the next status number
ref.api.d.addObject: All arguments are named. Put a class name, or a built-in shape name, in name. Keep the returned reference to control it later.
ref.api.d.setAnimation: Naming the clip that is already playing does nothing, so playback continues. Naming a different clip switches immediately.
ref.anim.name: Clip name
ref.anim.rootMotion: Whether to use the movement stored in the clip. Set false when your code decides the position
ref.m.setScreenSize: Set the internal resolution of the screen
ref.m.isKeyDown: Check whether a key is held down
ref.m.echo: Write to the footer. Each %@ is replaced by an argument
ref.m.echo.format: echo takes the same width and precision as printf: %[flags][width][.precision]@. So %.2@ gives two decimals, %08.2@ pads to eight characters with zeros, %-8@ aligns left and %+@ always shows the sign. The width counts the whole text, so four digits before and after the point is %09.4@. Without a precision the value is printed as it is — nothing gets silently cut.
ref.m.GLOBAL: Associative array shared across the whole game
ref.m.addCamera: Add a camera (replaces one with the same name)
ref.m.setCamera: Change settings; only the keys you write. Omitting the name targets the visible camera
ref.api.d.camera: Moving only the position just turns the camera. To follow something, move both the position and the target.
ref.cam.lens: Focal length in mm. Larger values zoom in
ref.cam.fov: Field of view in degrees, tied to the focal length
ref.m.addLight: Add a light (replaces one with the same name)
ref.m.setLight: Change settings; only the keys you write
ref.api.d.light: Up to four lights at once. Only one directional light can cast shadows; by default that is the light named sun.
ref.light.pos: Position. For a directional light, the offset to the target gives the direction
ref.light.range: How far a point light reaches
ref.ide.title: Using the IDE
ref.ide.d.project: The file icon in the header creates a project; the folder icon opens one. A project holds a code and an assets directory. Next time you open the app, the last project is restored automatically.
ref.ide.d.pane: The tabs at the top switch between kinds. "Add new" creates a class file or adds an asset. Thumbnails can be reordered by dragging, and the order is saved.
ref.tab.object.d: Class files. Click one to edit it on the right
ref.tab.sound.d: mp3, wav and so on. The play button previews them
ref.tab.model.d: glb, gltf. Hovering a thumbnail spins it
ref.key.save: Save the file you are editing
ref.key.run: Run the game (works while editing too)
ref.key.stop: Stop the game (ignored while the editor has focus)
ref.ide.d.keys: Esc is ignored in the editor because the vim key bindings use it to leave insert mode.
ref.ide.d.footer: The measured frame rate sits on the left, with the latest message beside it. Click to expand to ten lines and read back through the log, which keeps up to 1,000 lines.
ref.api.d.event: The argument of behavior carries information about the current frame. One is made per frame and handed to every object. You can also write behavior without the argument.
ref.event.frame: Frames since the game started (the first one is 0)
ref.event.time: Seconds since the game started. Derived from the frame count, so pauses and slow frames never make it jump
ref.hit.d: By default what you see is what collides, so you can start building without writing anything. Write a shape in @BOUNDARY only when you want to tune it — that detaches the hit area from the look. A huge-looking object can then carry a tiny hit area. Put null to give an object no hit area at all.
ref.hit.scale: When omitted, the area is 1×1×1 for a primitive, or the model's bounding box for 3D, multiplied by @SCALEX and friends. When you write the shape yourself, scaling does not apply and the size comes from width and the rest. Rotation never applies either way. Shapes that merely touch count as a hit.
ref.api.d.pad: Gamepad and keyboard states are mixed together into GAMEPAD. It is an array because several gamepads can be connected. Even with no gamepad, GAMEPAD[0] always exists so you can play with the keyboard.
ref.pad.cursor: The four directions, clockwise: up, right, down, left. On the keyboard, the arrow keys and WASD
ref.pad.button: Twelve buttons. On the keyboard, yuiohjklnm plus the comma and period. Some models have more buttons, but only the first twelve are used
ref.pad.axes: Analogue sticks. The first index is left or right stick, the second is X or Y. Values run -1.0 to 1.0, with 0 at the centre
ref.pad.value: 0.0 to 1.0. Analogue buttons report how far they are pressed
ref.pad.note: The keyboard mixes into GAMEPAD[0] only. A control counts as pressed if either source is pressed, and the larger value wins. Because layouts differ between models, the engine tries the standard layout, then a per-model preset, then works it out on the spot.
ref.pad.stick: Turning on stickAsCursor with setGamepadOption mixes the left stick's directions into the four-direction keys, so either one works. deadzone sets how far it must tilt to count as pressed (0.5 by default). The axes values stay available.
ref.pad.use: Write the controls your game uses in use, and the key config asks only for those. Only the kinds you write are covered; kinds you leave out are not asked. Even a pad with few buttons works, as long as the needed items are set. Anything the player chose to skip always reads 0.
ref.pad.config: Opens a screen where the player decides how their own pad is mapped. Just pressing what the screen asks for absorbs the differences between models. The setup is saved in the browser per game URL and is used automatically from then on.
ref.pad.config2: Controls you do not use can be left out with “Skip this item” (a skipped control always reads 0). Writing use narrows down what is asked. While setting up, nothing reaches the game. Esc, a click outside, or “Cancel” stops it. If no pad is found, press one of its buttons first — browsers hide a pad until it has been pressed once.
ref.hit.ask: You ask about collisions by naming the other side. The answer uses the positions at the moment you ask, so you can move, ask, and undo the move on the spot. You choose which method to use — @KIND does not decide it. The other side may also be an array. An object never hits itself.
ref.hit.intersect: Looks only at the XY plane, ignoring depth. For top-down and side-scrolling
ref.hit.collision: Looks at all of XYZ. For play in three dimensions
ref.hit.ret: The return value is the object you hit, or null when nothing was hit. That is more useful than a bare true, and reads the same inside an if. Given an array, it returns the first one hit. Both sides need a hit area for anything to register.
